newsitem.title: BELARUS: Chernomyrdin arrives for showdown in Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Chernomyrdin arrives for showdown in Belarus.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin arrived in Belarus on Thursday, hoping to defuse a standoff between President Alexander Lukashenko and his opponents over his plans to widen his powers by referendum.

With voting already under way and due to end on Sunday, the visit by Chernomyrdin was a last-ditch attempt by Russia to head off a destabilising conflict in the small post-Soviet republic, its closest ally.

Chernomyrdin arrived in the Belarussian capital around 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) and drove off to meet Lukashenko, who told a rally earlier in Brest he would under no circumstances back down over the referendum.
The Belarussian leader on Thursday faced a mounting chorus of international criticism, but diplomats said it was clear only Russia had the clout to make him soften his stand.

On Wednesday Lukashenko spurned peace talks organised by Moscow in the Russian city of Smolensk, where his chief opponent, parliament chairman Semyon Sharetsky, met leaders of Russia's two parliamentary chambers and agreed the outline of a compromise deal.
On Thursday he told a rally of 10,000 people in the main square of this western border city that it would be "laughable" for him to scrap the referendum.
"I am not going to share power with anyone," he declared in an interview with Russia's Interfax news agency.
His main demand is that parliament should abandon plans to impeach him.
The Belarus constitutional court, whose rulings the president has repeatedly ignored, is to meet on Friday to discuss the impeachment bid, launched by 70 deputies.

Lukashenko has the support of enough deputies to be able to stop the impeachment bid succeeding at the final stage. His opponents cannot muster the two-thirds majority of the 199 deputies required to remove him from office.
Lukashenko is seeking popular backing for major changes to the constitution which would extend his term by more than two years and tighten his grip on rival institutions.
"I will not give up this power...There must be order in the country...Power must be in strong hands to be strong, not in shaky, drunken hands," Lukashenko said on Wednesday.

The two parliamentary speakers, Yegor Stroyev of the Federation Council and Gennady Seleznyov of the State Duma, accompanied Chernomyrdin to Minsk in a rare show of unity between the Russian government and legislature.
After their arrival they went to parliament for talks with Sharetsky while Chernomyrdin saw Lukashenko. Talks involving all the parties were expected later.
Moscow, unlike western countries and some of Belarus's neighbours, has avoided any direct criticism of Lukashenko, who is the most pro-Russian of all leaders of post-Soviet states.

Despite his enthusiastic support for Moscow's goal of closer integration, the Belarussian leader's conflict with his opposition, his nostalgia for the Soviet Union and his hostility to economic reform have raised concern in Russia.

In the past week Lukashenko's prime minister has resigned and the president has sacked the head of the electoral commission, worsening his conflict with parliament whose leaders accuse him of trying to introduce a dictatorship.

Duma speaker Seleznyov told reporters in the Russian capital earlier that Moscow wanted Lukashenko to agree that the referendum on extending his powers should only be advisory, rather than binding, as he has insisted.

The future of the Belarussian constitution should be passed to a special constitutional committee, he said, adding that Lukashenko's parliamentary opponents would accept such a deal and were ready to drop their plans to impeach the president.
Russia's government and parliamentary leaders, meeting in Moscow on Thursday, agreed a joint approach to the crisis, calling for a compromise and strict compliance with the Belarussian constitution.
Meanwhile parliamentarians from 40 countries, meeting in Paris in the North Atlantic Assembly, demanded that the referendum be cancelled and urged Western governments not to recognise the result.
Neighbouring Poland's foreign minister said Lukashenko had clearly violated constitutional principles and that Warsaw wanted to avert undemocratic developments in Belarus.
Czech President Vaclav Havel, without mentioning Lukashenko, also voiced concern and Britain said it would summon the Belarussian ambassador to express its views on Friday.
